source.title: Emergent phases of superposition: from partial to full representation
source.authors: Li-Hao Guo; Yizhou Liu; Jeff Gore

record.tranche_reason: Tests feature representation and overlap in a trained toy network across widths and data statistics, using a different setup from the original sources. It does not measure neuron response selectivity in trained language or vision models.
record.gate_note: The study reports trained toy-model results on represented-feature counts, overlap relative to width, and the transition between partial and full representation. It does not test individual neurons' activation responses to different inputs, or whether such responses share a feature. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study characterizes superposition geometry in Anthropic's toy model: represented-feature counts versus width, and the partial-to-full representation transition. Its hidden layer is a linear bottleneck with no activation, so it has no privileged neuron basis. It never measures whether any neuron responds to several unrelated features. It therefore does not test whether neurons are polysemantic, or whether superposition causes neuron polysemanticity (V3). Superposition (r/m > 1) is a related but different construct from neuron polysemanticity. The findings belong under fits_no_version. No other version (vision or LM neurons, capacity-free polysemanticity, architecture effects, misread generalization, measurement dependence) is touched.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also report that the loss scaling changes across the transition. Below m*, loss grows linearly with Ē and depends weakly on width. Above m*, it grows roughly quadratically with Ē and decays as 1/m. Non-uniform firing probabilities delay the transition but lower the loss. They state extension to other architectures and losses remains unverified.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains an embedding–unembedding toy network with a ReLU output and mean-square reconstruction loss, varying width and feature statistics. It does not reproduce the neuron-interpretation methods of the cited original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The transition and critical width vary with model width, mean active-feature count, firing-probability non-uniformity, and activation-count variability. At strong firing-probability non-uniformity, the two-group representation description no longer applies.

fits_no_version.finding: In the ReLU-output toy model (n = 10000), the represented-feature count exceeds width at all tested widths (r/m > 1). Increasing width drives a continuous transition from partial to full representation. The critical width m* grows roughly as Ē log(n/Ē), and rises with firing non-uniformity and activation-count variance. The two-group picture breaks down at strong non-uniformity (ϵp = 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In toy superposition models, the number of features packed into the hidden space and whether all features get represented depend on width and data sparsity, with a phase transition at m* ~ Ē log(n/Ē).

record.problems: The evidence is from a toy network, not trained language or vision models, and does not measure neuron activation selectivity. Most settings use a single random seed; seed-to-seed deviations are described as too small to see and error bars are omitted in most figures. The authors also note limitations in their Gaussian crosstalk approximation and in the range of non-uniformity analyzed.
record.rows_left_out: Loss results were left out because they measure reconstruction loss rather than the representation overlap or neuron polysemanticity named in the claim. Detailed approximation and constrained-model comparisons were also left out because they do not add a separate result on the claim's represented-feature overlap.

untested.parts: All: no vision models or neuron responses.
Neuron-level polysemanticity and its causal link to superposition. Only feature-vector overlap in a neuron-free linear hidden space is measured.
All: no activation-function, architecture or regularization comparison.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all rows to V3 and gave supports/limits_scope labels. These are removed because the study never measures neurons. Its toy model has no nonlinearity in the hidden layer, so 'superposition' here means overlapping feature vectors, not polysemantic neurons. It cites Zoom In (an original source) only for the superposition hypothesis.

versions.untested_parts: Vision classifiers and individual neurons such as InceptionV1 4e:55.
Transformer language models, MLP neuron responses to tokens or contexts, and layer differences.

The study tests overlapping feature representations in a toy network, not whether individual neurons in trained language or vision models respond polysemantically, or whether superposition causally explains those responses.
No comparison tests polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
No comparison across activation functions, architectures, or regularization methods, and no performance-cost test of reducing polysemanticity.
No investigation of whether apparently mixed neuron responses share a feature or are related offshoots of one job.
No comparison of activation-range choices or explanation-scoring methods for classifying neurons as polysemantic.

rows.subject: Anthropic toy model of superposition
rows.operation_detail: Measured the ratio of represented features r to width m across widths.
rows.note: The text explicitly states that the represented-feature count exceeds the width at all tested widths in this setup.
rows.check: r/m > 1 shows feature-vector overlap (superposition) in a linear hidden space without neurons. It does not measure neuron polysemanticity, so it does not bear on V3's neuron-level causal claim. The state describes the study's own superposition measure only.

rows.subject: Anthropic toy model of superposition
rows.operation_detail: Measured the fraction r/n of represented features as width increased.
rows.value: Below 1 for m < m*; reaches 1 continuously for m > m*
rows.note: The authors describe partial representation below the critical width and full representation above it.
rows.check: The fraction of represented features r/n across width is a representation-completeness measure, not neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: Anthropic toy model of superposition
rows.size_stated: n = 10000 features in the main-text phase diagram
rows.operation_detail: Measured how the critical width for full representation changes with the mean active-feature count.
rows.value: In the limit 1 ≪ Ē ≪ n, m* ∼ Ē log(n/Ē); experiments are described as consistent with this scaling
rows.note: The reported relation concerns the width at which the model reaches full feature representation.
rows.check: Critical-width scaling m* ~ Ē log(n/Ē) concerns the full-representation transition, not neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: Anthropic toy model of superposition
rows.operation_detail: Measured the representation transition as firing-probability non-uniformity increased.
rows.note: The authors say the transition remains valid for moderate non-uniformity.
rows.check: The shift of m* with firing-probability non-uniformity is a superposition-phase result, not neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: Anthropic toy model of superposition
rows.operation_detail: Measured the transition as the variance in the number of active features increased.
rows.note: The paper says the partial-to-full transition remains valid in the tested parameter range.
rows.check: The shift of m* with activation-count variance is a superposition-phase result, not neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: Anthropic toy model of superposition
rows.operation_detail: Examined whether feature-vector norms separate into represented and unrepresented groups.
rows.baseline: Moderate ϵp, where two norm bands are reported
rows.value: At ϵp = 2, the bands merge even at small m; norms vary continuously with feature index
rows.note: The authors state that features cannot be divided into represented and unrepresented groups in this regime, and that the partial-representation approximation no longer applies.
rows.check: Breakdown of the two-group norm description at ϵp = 2 concerns the applicability of the authors' approximation. It says nothing about neuron polysemanticity. 'Absent' only makes sense relative to the study's own bimodality measure.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Uniform features, n = 10000, Ē = 50; and the reported width-versus-sparsity phase diagram
reader_labels.reason: The trained toy model has r/m > 1 across tested widths, and the represented-feature fraction rises to full representation as width increases (r1–r3).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Moderate firing-probability non-uniformity and tested activation-count variability
reader_labels.reason: The representation transition persists, while its critical width changes with non-uniformity and activation-count variability (r4–r5).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Strong firing-probability non-uniformity, Ē = 1 and ϵp = 2.0
reader_labels.reason: The two-group partial-representation description breaks down in this tested regime (r6).
